turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Morning. I brought Mr Keane in, the letter said a kidney review.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. Umm this computer is after freezing on me. Sorry, say the name again?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Patrick Keane. Umm I'm only here for the bloods, the kidney ones. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, the kidney bloods are up. Creatinine is 168, and the eGFR is down at 36.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Last year your one in the hospital said the kidney blood was borderline. I don't know if 36 is desperate, doctor.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the screen jumped. Who said borderline, say it again?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): The hospital kidney doctor, last year. Just borderline. I haven't a clue of the figure.
[SEG0008] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He lives on his own. I call in the mornings and do the tablet box. The numbers do upset him.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. The tablets, what are you on? Slowly, I'm still catching the screen.

[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Amlodipine for the pressure, in the mornings. Metforman for the sugar, that's the diabetes. Ramiprill as well, they said don't ever stop it. The kidney trouble is there too.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Doses. I missed them. Amlodipine, what strength?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Err I don't know, doctor. The white one.
[SEG0013] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Amlodipine 5 milligrams every morning. Metformin 500 with breakfast and with the tea. Ramipril 5 milligrams at night.
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): And the cholesterol one at night. A small yellow yoke. I don't know the name of it, doctor.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yellow cholesterol tablet at night, name unknown. Any herbs, or stuff from the shop?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Only the ayurvedic powder in the morning. A spoon of it in the tea. My sister sends it over.
[SEG0017] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He's buying ibuprofin in the shop though. Two of the 400s when the knee is at him. I told him to leave them be.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Again, two of the what? The screen ate that.
[SEG0019] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Two 400 milligram ibuprofen. Most days, when the knee pains him. From the shop, not on a prescription.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): The knee is desperate, doctor. I'm after overdoing it in the garden, that's all. Sure I can't hear myself think with that radio outside.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Any chest pain?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I'm not breathless.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the ankles, any swelling?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are the bowels? And the waterworks?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Bowels are grand. I get up once in the night to pass water. I don't know, doctor, does that count?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Once is nothing unusual. How's the energy in yourself?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): I feel like a wet rag. No energy at all. And I've a frog in my throat this week, croaky as anything.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again. A frog in the throat?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Croaky all this week. And my feet feel dead, both of them, like they're not mine.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Numb, the two feet. How long would that be?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh I don't know, doctor. A long while. I can't give you a date.
[SEG0035] person_1 (CAREGIVER): First I heard of the feet. The ankles swell every evening though, I've seen them myself.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): You said no swelling a minute ago. Is it every evening or not?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Well actually they come up of an evening, like sausages. I put the feet up and it eases. I forgot, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm looking. Both ankles are puffy and the thumb leaves a little dent, mild enough. Blood pressure today is 146 over 82.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Is that the tablets doing it? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working impression is the shop ibuprofen is pulling the kidney function down, with the diabetes and the ramipril in the mix. Creatinine 168 and an eGFR of 36 would fit that. It's not confirmed.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): So do I stop the ramiprill?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. Continue the ramipril, 5 milligrams at night. Stop the ibuprofen, nothing from the shop or the chemist, none of that family.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): What about the knee then, and the powder? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Start paracetamol, two 500 milligram tablets up to four times in the day. Leave the ayurvedic powder off, there's no telling what's in it. I'll book repeat creatinine and eGFR in two weeks, and I'll see you back in a fortnight.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): And if the knee is still desperate?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the paracetamol isn't holding the knee, we might do an x-ray. I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0047] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Can I say, I'm not sure he takes the ramipril every night. Some mornings the tablet is still in the blister.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): The ramipril. Say that again?
[SEG0049] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He misses nights. I can't say he takes it the way it's written.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): Most nights I do. Sometimes I forget. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Try for every night, the kidneys need it. If the ankles get worse or you get breathless before the fortnight, come back sooner.
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): Grand so. I'll do my best.

spec.situation: Older diabetic with kidney disease on review; creatinine and eGFR read aloud; takes ibuprofen from a shop against advice; ramipril continued, painkiller advice changed.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

traps.happens: The patient lists medicines with their purpose ('amlodipine for the pressure', 'the cholesterol one at night', 'sugar tablets') and also mentions a herbal or shop remedy in passing ('only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning'). Their chronic conditions are never asked about directly.
traps.label_rule: Each medicine is recorded with the dose and timing said for THAT medicine; the herbal remedy is a medicine too (currently_used). A condition the patient states through its medicine ('for the pressure') is a past_medical_history entry ONLY if the patient actually said the condition name or its everyday name ('the pressure' = hypertension, normalized); do not invent a duration.

features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Caregiver reports two 400 mg ibuprofen most days for knee pain; fact's dose omits total 800 mg.
bad.text: ibuprofen (dose=400 mg, frequency=2 tablets most days, indication=knee pain, status=currently_used, reported_by=caregiver)

bad.text: paracetamol (dose=500 mg, frequency=2 tablets up to 4 times daily, indication=knee pain, status=planned, reported_by=doctor)

bad.reason: Patient mentions prior hospital kidney blood test; he did not request it.
bad.text: previous hospital kidney blood test (type=laboratory, status=completed, requested_by=patient, indication=reported as borderline last year)

bad.reason: Action supported, but dose is incomplete: doctor prescribed two 500 mg tablets each dose.

omissions.text: Ibuprofen dose is recorded inaccurately: caregiver said he takes two 400 mg tablets most days for knee pain (800 mg per dose), not 400 mg.
Negative finding asked and answered but not recorded: no ankle swelling was initially denied by the patient before later clarification that swelling occurs in the evenings.
